title: Frontend Performance Optimization: A Practical Playbook
excerpt: A senior-level guide to measuring what matters, reducing load and render cost, and shipping faster Vue and Nuxt experiences without guessing.
body: ## Why performance is a product decision Users do not experience "frameworks" — they experience waiting. A slow first paint, a layout shift under a button, or a janky scroll all communicate the same thing: the product is not ready for them. Performance work is most effective when it is treated as engineering discipline, not a last-minute Lighthouse chase. The goal is simple: **make the critical path short, keep the main thread free, and measure continuously** so regressions cannot hide in a large frontend codebase. ## Start with measurement, not intuition Optimize against numbers, not vibes. Before rewriting a component tree or swapping libraries, establish a baseline: 1. **Lab data** — Lighthouse / DevTools Performance for reproducible profiles. 2. **Field data** — real-user metrics (CrUX or your own RUM) for how people actually experience the site. 3. **Budgets** — explicit ceilings for JS weight, LCP element size, and long tasks. ### Core Web Vitals as a shared language Google's Core Web Vitals give teams a shared vocabulary for user-centric quality: - **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)** — when the main content becomes visible. - **INP (Interaction to Next Paint)** — how quickly the UI responds to input. - **CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)** — how stable the layout stays while loading. Treat these as *symptoms*. A poor LCP usually points to late discovery of the hero image, render-blocking CSS/fonts, or a heavy client bundle delaying hydration. A poor INP usually points to long tasks on the main thread. CLS usually points to images or embeds without reserved space, late-injected UI, or web fonts that reflow text. > If you cannot explain which resource or script caused the regression, you are not done profiling. ## Loading strategy: get the first screen out of the way ### Images Images are still the most common LCP candidates on marketing and portfolio surfaces. - Serve modern formats (`webp` / `avif`) with sensible quality. - Always set **width and height** (or CSS aspect-ratio) to prevent CLS. - Use `loading="lazy"` for below-the-fold media; **eager** (or priority hints) for the LCP image. - Prefer responsive `srcset` / `sizes` so mobile does not download a desktop asset. In Nuxt, `@nuxt/image` already encodes many of these defaults — use it consistently instead of ad-hoc `` tags for content imagery. ### Fonts Fonts often block rendering or cause late text shifts. - Limit families and weights to what the UI actually uses. - Prefer `font-display: swap` (or optional) with a metric-matched fallback to reduce CLS. - Self-host when possible so font requests share the site's connection and caching policy. ### JavaScript JS is the most expensive resource you ship: it must be downloaded, parsed, compiled, and executed. - **Code-split by route** so visitors to `/blog` do not pay for the contact form's validation stack. - Defer non-critical interactivity (analytics, chat widgets, decorative motion) until after hydration or idle. - Audit dependencies — a single convenience library can cost tens of kilobytes for one helper function. - Prefer progressive enhancement: static HTML first, interactivity second. For Vue and Nuxt specifically: - Keep client-only plugins genuinely client-only. - Use lazy-loaded components for heavy, below-the-fold UI. - Avoid shipping large chart or editor libraries on pages that never use them. ## Rendering cost: respect the main thread A fast network does not fix a busy main thread. After the bytes arrive, the browser still has to style, layout, paint, and run your framework. Practical habits that compound: - Prefer **CSS transforms and opacity** for motion; avoid animating layout properties. - Honor `prefers-reduced-motion` — accessibility and performance often align. - Virtualize long lists; do not mount hundreds of DOM nodes "just in case." - Batch DOM reads/writes; layout thrashing is still a real footgun in complex dashboards. - Memoization is not free — measure before sprinkling `computed` complexity or hand-rolled caches. When profiling in Chrome DevTools, look for **long tasks** (>50ms). Break them up with `scheduler.yield` / idle callbacks where appropriate, or move pure work off the critical path. ## A repeatable optimization loop Use the same loop on every feature: 1. **Reproduce** the slow path on a throttled CPU/network profile. 2. **Attribute** the cost (network waterfall, main-thread flame chart, or layout shift regions). 3. **Fix the bottleneck** with the smallest change that moves the metric. 4. **Re-measure** against the same profile and against a budget. 5. **Guard** with CI or a manual checklist so the fix does not regress next sprint. This is how performance becomes a habit instead of a hero project. ## What "good" looks like on a portfolio site For a content-heavy personal site, a professional bar usually means: - Fast LCP on a mid-tier mobile device over a realistic network. - Near-zero CLS on article and project pages. - Minimal JS on read-only routes (blog posts should feel like documents). - Predictable fonts and reserved media boxes. - Clear ownership: every new dependency has a weight justification. Performance is not about chasing a perfect score. It is about **respecting the user's time** and shipping interfaces that feel deliberate under real conditions. ## Takeaways - Measure with Core Web Vitals and profiles before rewriting architecture. - Attack LCP with image, font, and critical-path JS discipline. - Protect INP by keeping the main thread free of long tasks. - Prevent CLS with stable layout for media, embeds, and typography. - Make performance part of the definition of done — not a cleanup pass before launch.
